passage:
Note to Ujjwal's parents, from Hansa, kindergarten teacher
Today Ujjwal told a visiting uncle, "Your cat drawing looks like a potato." He wasn't being cruel; he looked puzzled when the uncle's smile slipped. At line-up he would not let two older boys cut in. "That's not fair. We were here first." He stood his ground even when they glared. We practised saying a true thing in a kinder way: "I think the cat needs pointy ears." He tried it twice, grinning. His honesty and grit are real strengths; the tone is what we are working on together.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say the visiting uncle's cat drawing looked like?
qa.a: He said it looks like a potato.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's puzzled look suggest when the uncle's smile slipped?
qa.a: It suggests he said what he honestly thought and didn't expect it to hurt.

qa.q: What did Hansa try with Ujjwal after the potato comment?
qa.a: Hansa practised saying the same true thing more kindly, like suggesting pointy ears, and he tried it twice.

qa.q: How might the two older boys see Ujjwal after he stopped them cutting in?
qa.a: They may be annoyed, but they also learn he will not give way when something is unfair.

grounding: A teacher notes a blunt, fairness-minded young child and guides him toward a kinder tone without crushing his honesty.

passage: At the weekly haat, six-year-old Sachin watched the man weighing their onions. "Your scale is crooked," he announced. His elder brother Vijay went red. The seller laughed and checked it; the pan was sticking. On the walk home Vijay split the guavas: three for himself, two for Sachin. Sachin stopped in the dusty road. "That's not fair. You always take more." "I'm older." "Older doesn't eat more guavas." When Vijay walked on, Sachin sat down. Finally Vijay gave him one. "You're right," he said, "but say it without shouting next time." Sachin thought. "Okay. Quieter. Still fair."

qa.q: What did Sachin say about the seller's scale?
qa.a: He said, "Your scale is crooked."

qa.q: Why did Sachin sit down in the dusty road?
qa.a: He felt strongly that the guava split was unfair and was determined not to give way.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Sachin to change, and how did Sachin respond?
qa.a: Vijay agreed he was right but asked him not to shout; Sachin agreed to be quieter but still fair.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Sachin called out the seller's scale?
qa.a: He went red, so he was probably embarrassed, even though Sachin turned out to be right.

grounding: A six-year-old says exactly what he thinks and argues for fairness, and his brother guides him toward a gentler tone.

passage: At his cousin's birthday in their Pune society hall, Lokesh took one bite of cake and announced, 'This is too sweet. I don't like it.' The aunty who baked it laughed awkwardly. Later, when two big boys pushed to the front of the game line, Lokesh planted his feet. 'No. There's a line. Go back.' They went back. Walking home, his papa Vikas said, 'You were right about the line. Strong.' Lokesh grinned. 'And the cake?' 'True, maybe. But Aunty worked hard. You could say, thank you, it's very sweet for me.' 'Still true?' 'Still true. Just kinder.'

qa.q: What did Lokesh say about the cake?
qa.a: 'This is too sweet. I don't like it.'

qa.q: What does Lokesh planting his feet in the line show?
qa.a: He felt determined and sure about fairness, not scared of the big boys.

qa.q: How did Vikas guide Lokesh?
qa.a: He praised the honesty about the line and showed a kinder way to say the truth about the cake: 'thank you, it's very sweet for me.'

qa.q: How might the aunty who baked the cake have felt?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit hurt or embarrassed, laughing awkwardly at the blunt remark.

grounding: Shows a young child who says exactly what he thinks and stands up for fairness, and a parent guiding him toward a kinder tone.

passage:
'Dhruv took four green and I only got one. That's not fair!'
'I needed green for my tree,' Dhruv said.
'I need green for my frog. You're greedy.'
Mumma looked up. 'Nandini.'
'He is! I'm just saying the truth.'
'You're right that it isn't fair. Greedy is a hurting word, though. Try again.'
Nandini scowled, then folded her arms. 'Dhruv. Please give me two green. Then we're equal.'
Dhruv slid two across. 'Fine.'
'Thank you,' Nandini said, still scowling a little. 'Now my frog can be green.'

qa.q: How many green crayons did Dhruv take?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she called Dhruv greedy?
qa.a: She felt angry and certain it was unfair, and determined to say so.

qa.q: What did Mumma get right?
qa.a: She agreed it wasn't fair but asked for a kinder word, so Nandini kept her honesty and changed her tone.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel being called greedy?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt stung and defensive, since he did need green for his tree.

grounding: Shows a young child who argues bluntly for fairness and won't give way, and a parent guiding her toward a kinder tone.

passage:
Note to Vasudha's parents
Vasudha had a strong day. When our visiting artist showed a cat drawing, Vasudha said loudly, 'That looks like a dog.' Some children giggled and the moment went flat. At snack time she noticed the boys' table had more fruit and told our helper, 'That's not fair. Count them.' She was right, and would not sit until it was fixed. I told her I was proud she spoke up. We also practised 'I think' instead of 'That is'. Her honesty is a gift; we're working on her tone.
Sharmila, class teacher

qa.q: What did Vasudha notice at snack time?
qa.a: That the boys' table had more fruit.

qa.q: What does Vasudha refusing to sit until the fruit was fixed show?
qa.a: She felt strongly about fairness and was determined, not willing to give way.

qa.q: How does the 'I think' practice help Vasudha?
qa.a: It keeps her honest opinion but softens the tone, so she can say what she thinks more kindly.

qa.q: How might the visiting artist have felt?
qa.a: The artist may have felt a little awkward and deflated as the children giggled and the moment went flat.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a young child who speaks bluntly and argues for fairness, with an adult guiding her toward a kinder tone.

passage: At the village well, Bhavna, six, marched up to a big boy who had pushed his bucket ahead of hers. "You pushed in! That's not fair. I was here first." The boy blinked and stepped back. At lunch she told her grandmother, Vandana, "Your roti is burnt on this side." Vandana laughed. "You're right. But how could you say it so I'd feel nice?" Bhavna frowned, thinking hard. "Dadi, this side is a little burnt, but the other side is yummy?" "Much better." Bhavna nodded, satisfied, and ate the good side first.

qa.q: What did the big boy do at the well?
qa.a: He pushed his bucket ahead of Bhavna's.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when the boy pushed in?
qa.a: She felt angry at the unfairness and determined to stand up for herself.

qa.q: How did Vandana guide Bhavna?
qa.a: She agreed Bhavna was right but helped her find a kinder way to say the same honest thing.

qa.q: How might the big boy have felt when Bhavna challenged him?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, stepping back.

grounding: Shows a blunt, determined child who argues for fairness and says what she thinks, and a grandmother guiding her toward kindness in tone.
